descriptionChirho: Something or someone that is known, recognized, or notable -- used predicatively or attributively to describe facts, events, miracles, or persons that are publicly recognized or well-known. The 'notable miracle' usage (Acts 4:16) and general 'known' usage share the core semantic of being within public awareness. Spanish uses 'conocido/conocidas/notable' (known/notable); Hindi uses 'ज्ञात/जाना-पहचाना/चिह्न' (gyat/jana-pahchana, known/recognized); Arabic uses 'معلوم/معلومة' (ma'lum, known); Korean uses '알려졌다/표적' (allyeojyeotda, was made known / pyojeok, sign); Swahili uses 'inajulikana' (it is known) for both senses.

A person who is known to someone, used substantivally to denote personal acquaintances or familiar associates, as distinct from strangers or intimate family. This substantival usage represents a distinct sense from the adjectival 'known.' Spanish uses 'conocidos' (acquaintances); Hindi uses 'जान-पहचानों/जानने वाले' (jan-pahchanon/janne vale, known ones/those who know); Arabic uses 'معارفه/المعارف' (ma'arifihi/al-ma'arif, his acquaintances/the acquaintances); Korean uses '아는 자들' (aneun jadeul, those who know); Swahili uses 'wajuaana/marafiki' (acquaintances/friends).
